This article goes through the package one function at a time. For each
function it says why you would use it, what it does, what it returns, and which
arguments change the answer. It ends with three short applications that show
how much a result moves when you change the currency or the rank you report
at. Everything runs offline on the invented example table that ships with the
package: 24 prey records from 11 stomachs of three predators. The numbers show
the mechanics, not the diet of these fish.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## The pipeline

DietView is a short pipeline. Every step returns an object you can print,
inspect and save.

| Step | Function | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| Declare | `dv_spec()` | `dietview_spec`: which column plays which role |
| Check | `dv_validate()` | the data, invisibly, with messages about it |
| Prepare | `dv_prepare()` | `dietview_prep`: data, taxonomy and matching log |
| Review | `dv_taxonomy_report()` | the matches that need a look |
| Count | `dv_build_tree()` | `dietview_tree`: one row per node, with records, weight and shares |
| Read | `dv_rank_table()` | the rows of one ring |
| Draw | `dv_sunburst()` | a plotly figure |
| Share | `dv_build_html()`, `run_dietview()`, `dv_deploy()` | an HTML file, a Shiny app, a deployed file |

Two helpers (`dv_add_period()`, `dv_size_bins()`) build covariates,
`dv_palette()` sets the colors, `dv_digestion_diagnostic()` relates
identification depth to digestion, and `dv_species_card_assets()` finds a photo
and a description for a predator.

```{r load}
dat <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)
lineage <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)

str(dat, vec.len = 2, give.attr = FALSE)
```

One row is one prey record: one prey taxon found in one stomach. There are no
`kingdom` to `species` columns; DietView adds them.

## `dv_spec()`: declare your columns once

**Why.** Every survey names its columns differently. Instead of renaming them
before the analysis, which leaves published code working on a table that no
longer matches the archived data, you record which column plays which role.
The original table stays as it is, and the specification can be printed,
archived and compared between studies.

**What it does.** It stores the mapping and nothing else. Your data are not
touched.

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator   = "predator_species_common_name",
  stomach    = "stomach_id",
  prey_id    = "aphia_id",
  prey_name  = "verified_name",
  weight     = "prey_weight",
  digestion  = "digestion_level_id",
  covariates = c("period", "size_class", "region")
)

str(spec)
```

**Arguments that matter.**

*`prey_id` is used before `prey_name`.* Give both when you have both. The ID is
used for the lookup, and the name lets DietView check that the two agree. When
a record has no ID, its name is used.

*`prey_name` must be the scientific name*, because it is sent to WoRMS, which
does not know common names. A common name either fails to match or, with
fuzzy matching, can match a wrong taxon. The predator, by contrast, is never
looked up: it is only a grouping and display label, so a common name is fine.

*The name does not have to be a species.* `Decapoda`, `Amphipoda` and
`Teleostei` are valid values: they record the rank at which identification
stopped. Do not replace them with a guessed species; DietView shows such
records as unidentified below the rank they reached.

*`ranks` defaults to seven ranks*, kingdom to species. Shorten it if your prey
are never identified past family; the sunburst then has fewer rings.

*`covariates` lists what you can later compare diets across.* Declaring a
column costs nothing.

*`count`* declares a column of individuals per record, for the numerical share
(%N). It is left out here. If you declare it, build trees with
`dv_tree(prep, "numbers")` when you want %N, and note that records without a
count, usually the unidentified material, then contribute nothing.

## `dv_validate()`: check the table before anything else

Run `dv_validate()` before anything else. It stops if a column you declared is
missing, if there is no prey key column or if a weight is negative. It warns
if weights are not numbers, if records have no prey key or if stomach IDs
repeat across predators, and it ends with a one-line description of the
sample: how many records, stomachs and predators, and how many records lack a
weight. It never changes your data.

```{r validate, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE}
dv_validate(dat, spec)
```

**What you get back.** The data, invisibly, with the counts in the
`dv_report` attribute. The information is in the messages and warnings.

**Arguments that matter.** With `strict_covariates = FALSE`, a declared
covariate missing from the data is dropped from the specification with a
warning instead of stopping. `dv_prepare()` takes the same argument.

## `dv_prepare()`: attach the taxonomy, and log how

**Why.** Here prey are placed in a taxonomic hierarchy taken from an external
authority or from a lineage table you supply, instead of being grouped by hand.
Two surveys prepared against the same authority can then be compared without
recoding.

**What it does.** It validates the table, looks up each distinct prey key,
joins the lineage back to every record, and leaves the ranks below the last
identified rank empty.

```{r prepare}
prep <- dv_prepare(
  dat, spec,
  taxonomy = "table",   # offline: use the lineage table supplied
  lineage  = lineage,
  verbose  = FALSE
)

class(prep)
names(prep)
```

**What you get back.** A `dietview_prep` list. Its main components are:

- `data`: your table plus one column per rank;
- `spec`: the specification;
- `ranks`: the ranks used;
- `taxonomy_log`: on the WoRMS path, one row per distinct prey with how it was
  matched.

```{r prep-ranks}
prep$ranks
head(prep$data[, c("verified_name", prep$ranks)], 4)
```

**Arguments that matter.**

*`taxonomy` chooses the source.*

| Value | Behavior | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `"auto"` | use rank columns if present, else the lineage table if one is given, else WoRMS | quick exploration |
| `"columns"` | use rank columns already in the data | taxonomy resolved elsewhere |
| `"worms"` | query WoRMS online | first pass on a new dataset |
| `"table"` | join a lineage table you supply | reruns, offline work, non-marine prey |

*Resolve once, then freeze.* Run once with `taxonomy = "worms"`, read the log,
save the resulting lineage table, and use `taxonomy = "table"` for every later
run. Later runs are then offline and fast, and they use one fixed taxonomic
snapshot. Different versions of an authority can return different lineages, so
an archived lineage table plays the same role for the taxonomy as a lockfile
does for package versions.

*`fuzzy = TRUE` has a cost.* It can match a misspelled name, and it can also
match a different taxon whose name is close. Every such match is logged with
`match_type = "fuzzy"`, and you need to read the log to catch the wrong ones.

*The number of lookups depends on the number of distinct prey, not on the
number of records.* Two million records with three thousand distinct prey
need three thousand lookups.

## `dv_taxonomy_report()`: read the log before you plot

**Why.** Fuzzy and unresolved matches are where a diet description most often
goes wrong without anyone noticing.

**What it does.** It returns the rows of the matching log that need a look,
largest number of records first.

```{r taxreport, eval = FALSE}
prep_online <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")

dv_taxonomy_report(prep_online, which = "review")   # the matches to check
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_online, which = "all",      # the whole log, to archive
                   file = file.path(tempdir(), "taxonomy_log.csv"))
```

The log exists only on the WoRMS path. A `prep` built with `taxonomy = "table"`,
as everywhere else in this article, has no matching history, because you did
the matching when you built the table, and this function stops with a message
saying so. The review therefore belongs to the one online run in the
resolve-once-then-freeze workflow, not to every rerun.

`which = "review"` (the default) returns fuzzy and unresolved matches,
unaccepted IDs that were replaced by their accepted ID, IDs that could not be
checked, names that differ from the name WoRMS holds for their ID, and prey
whose classification could not be retrieved. `"fuzzy"` and `"unresolved"`
return one of those groups; `"all"` returns the whole log. Pass `file` to write
it out.

An unresolved prey is not always an error. In this table
"unidentified material" has no AphiaID and no taxonomic name, so it should not
match anything; its records are unidentified at every rank. The unresolved
prey you did not expect are the ones to chase.

## `dv_build_tree()`: count the diet at every rank

**Why.** This is where the shares at every rank are computed.

**What it does.** It counts at the finest rank and adds up toward the
kingdom. Each node carries three values: `value_item` (the number of distinct
prey items below it), `value_occ` (the number of prey records) and `value_w`
(the summed weight). Dividing by the total gives `pct_occ` and `pct_w`.

```{r tree}
tree <- dv_build_tree(
  prep$data,
  ranks      = prep$ranks,
  weight_col = spec$weight
)

head(tree, 4)
```

**What you get back.** A `dietview_tree` data frame with `id`, `label`,
`parent`, `rank`, the three values and the two shares.

Every record has one place in every ring: under the taxon it was identified to
at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, in an unidentified node
below the last rank it reached. Two properties follow, and it is worth checking
them once:

```{r invariants}
# 1. every ring holds all the records, so each sums to 100%
round(tapply(tree$pct_occ, tree$rank, sum), 6)

# 2. a parent's value equals the sum of its children's (largest gap: 0)
kid_sums <- tapply(tree$value_occ, tree$parent, sum)
parents  <- intersect(tree$id, names(kid_sums))
max(abs(tree$value_occ[match(parents, tree$id)] - kid_sums[parents]))
```

The first lets you read any ring on its own. The second is what lets the rings
nest in a sunburst. Because every ring holds the same records, the denominator
is the same at every rank: here all `r nrow(prep$data)` records.

**Arguments that matter.**

*`weight_col = NULL` is allowed* and leaves the weight view empty. The share
of prey records still works. Use it when weights are too sparse to trust.

*`count_col` changes what one record counts for.* Left `NULL`, each record
counts once and `pct_occ` is the share of prey records. Given a column of
counts, each record counts its number of individuals and `pct_occ` becomes the
numerical share (%N). `dv_tree(prep, "numbers")` does this from the
specification. Say in your methods which one you used.

*`value_occ` counts prey records, not stomachs.* This is the quantity most
likely to be misread. Its share is not the frequency of occurrence (%FO) of the
diet literature, which is the share of stomachs containing a prey. %FO does not
add up from children to parent: a stomach holding two species of one genus
counts once for the genus and once for each species. A nested sunburst needs
values that add up, so it cannot show %FO. Use `dv_fo_table()` for %FO, and
report each quantity under its own name.

## `dv_rank_table()`: the numbers behind one ring

**Why.** A figure is for looking; a table is for reporting and checking.

**What it does.** It returns the rows of one rank, sorted by share of prey
records, with the unidentified rows included.

```{r ranktable}
dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")
```

Rank labels are title case (`"Class"`, `"Family"`, `"Genus"`), built from the
specification's `ranks`. The rows labeled `NA` are the records unidentified at
this rank, one row per parent. Keep them: dropping them would rescale the
remaining shares to the identified records only.

## `dv_sunburst()`: the whole diet in one figure

**Why.** A taxonomy is a hierarchy, and a bar chart shows one rank at a time.
A sunburst shows every rank at once.

**What it does.** It draws the tree, with records unidentified at a rank in
white wedges with gray edges.

```{r sunburst-occ}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")
```

**Arguments that matter.**

*`mode` chooses what sizes the wedges:* `"occurrence"` (prey records),
`"weight"` or `"count"` (distinct prey items). Records and weight often rank
prey differently (see Application 1), so look at both.

*`colors` matters as soon as you compare panels.* Left `NULL`, each call builds
its own palette from its own labels, so a panel with 12 taxa and one with 9 can
give the same taxon different colors. Build one palette from the pooled tree and
pass it to every panel:

```{r global-palette}
colors <- dv_palette(tree$label)   # from the pooled tree: covers every taxon
head(colors, 4)
colors["NA"]                       # unidentified is always white
```

`run_dietview()` and `dv_build_html()` do this for you. You only need to do it
when you draw panels yourself.

*`rotation = 90` puts the start angle at the top*, and the figure keeps the
node order from `dv_build_tree()` instead of sorting wedges by size. Panels
therefore start at the same angle and list taxa in the same order.

That does not keep a taxon at the same angle in every panel. If a taxon is
absent from one stratum, the wedges after it move round to close the gap. Use
color, not position, to find a taxon across panels.

## `dv_palette()`: colors, and white for unidentified records

**Why.** Across panels, a taxon is recognized by its color, and unidentified
records need to look different from everything else.

**What it does.** It gives each label a color from a 20-color palette and
makes `"NA"` white. With more than 20 taxa, colors are reused, so check the
hover labels before you read a color as a taxon.

Build it from the pooled tree, not from one stratum: only the pooled tree is
sure to contain every taxon.

## `dv_add_period()` and `dv_size_bins()`: covariates in one line

**Why.** Predator size is one of the strongest structuring variables in fish
diets, partly through gape limitation (Scharf et al. 2000). A diet averaged
over a predator's whole size range mixes what small and large individuals eat,
so it is worth splitting by size.

```{r covariates}
dat$period2   <- dv_add_period(dat$year, breaks = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2025))
dat$size_bin2 <- dv_size_bins(dat$somatic_length_cm, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 200))

table(dat$period2, useNA = "ifany")
table(dat$size_bin2, useNA = "ifany")
```

**Arguments that matter.** `dv_add_period()` labels each period with the years
it contains, such as `"2001-2010"`, unless you pass `labels`; a year equal to an
inner break belongs to the earlier period. `dv_size_bins()` uses
`right = FALSE` by default, so bins include their lower edge (`"[0, 30)"`) and
a fish of exactly 30 cm falls in the second bin. A value outside the breaks
gets no level. Choose breaks on biology (maturity, gape) rather than on
quantiles, and state them in your methods.

## `dv_digestion_diagnostic()`: identification depth and digestion

**Why.** Digestion affects both what can still be identified and what is left
to weigh. A table of identification depth by digestion score is what Buckland
et al. (2017) asked diet studies to report.

**What it does.** It cross-tabulates the digestion score against the deepest
rank each record was identified to, in records and in weight.

```{r digestion}
dg <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
head(dg, 8)
```

**What you get back.** A data frame with `digestion`, `finest_rank`,
`n_records`, `weight`, and the percentages within each digestion score,
`p_records` and `p_weight`.

**Arguments that matter.** Percentages are computed within each digestion
score, so each score adds up to 100 whatever its sample size; always read them
next to `n_records`. Pass `by` to split the table by a covariate when you
suspect the profile differs between strata. A steep profile is a reason to be
cautious with the weight currency in particular. The vignette "Identification
depth and digestion" explains how to read the table.

## `dv_taxonomy_worms()`: the WoRMS lookup on its own

**Why.** `dv_prepare(taxonomy = "worms")` calls it for you. Call it directly to
build the lineage table you will freeze.

**What it does.** It takes a data frame of distinct prey keys and returns
their lineages and how each was matched. It tries, in order: retrieval by
AphiaID, the accepted ID behind an unaccepted name, exact name match, then
fuzzy match.

```{r worms, eval = FALSE}
keys <- unique(dat[, c("aphia_id", "verified_name")])
names(keys) <- c("prey_id", "prey_name")

tax <- dv_taxonomy_worms(keys, fuzzy = TRUE)

table(tax$match_type)
write.csv(tax, "my_lineage.csv", row.names = FALSE)   # freeze it
```

**Arguments that matter.** It expects columns named `prey_id` and `prey_name`,
one row per distinct prey, not your full record table. Each row carries its
`match_type` and `matched_name`, so you can correct a fuzzy match by hand
before you save the lineage. Successful lookups are cached under `cache_dir`,
so a rerun after correcting a spelling only queries what changed. Failed
lookups are not cached.

## `dv_species_card_assets()`: a photo and a description for a predator

**Why.** People who read a dashboard often need to recognize the predators,
not only read their diets: technicians, students new to the fauna, managers.

```{r cards, eval = FALSE}
dv_species_card_assets(
  predator  = "Atlantic cod",
  latin     = "Gadus morhua",
  photo_source = "inaturalist",
  image_dir = tempdir()
)
```

**Arguments that matter.** It works for one predator at a time.
`photo_source` is `"none"` (the default), `"inaturalist"` or `"wikipedia"`;
with `"none"` the card has no photo and no description unless you supply them
in `species_info`. With iNaturalist, only photos whose license is in
`licenses` (by default CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA) are used, and the result carries
the photographer, the license and the photo's page. Photos are embedded in the HTML file, so the dashboard
keeps working when `image_dir` is deleted. The article on species cards
covers image licenses.

## `dv_build_html()`, `run_dietview()`, `dv_deploy()`: sharing the result

**Why.** Many of the people who need a diet description do not use R. A
single HTML file reaches them without a running R session.

```{r ship, eval = FALSE}
# one HTML file that opens in any browser, without R
dv_build_html(
  prep,
  output = file.path(tempdir(), "dietview.html"),
  strata = c("period", "size_class"),
  cross  = list(c("size_class", "period"))   # inner, outer
)

# interactive exploration
run_dietview(prep)
```

**Arguments that matter.** `cross = list(c(inner, outer))` reads "inner within
outer": one row per level of `outer`, one sunburst per level of `inner`.
Crossing multiplies panels: two covariates with four levels each give sixteen
sunbursts.

A dashboard is a snapshot: it holds the data as they were when you built it.
That is a limit for monitoring and an advantage for archiving.

## Application 1: records and weight disagree

Same tree, same records, two currencies.

```{r app-currencies}
cls <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")

data.frame(
  taxon       = cls$label,
  records_pct = round(cls$pct_occ, 1),
  weight_pct  = round(cls$pct_w, 1),
  difference  = round(cls$pct_w - cls$pct_occ, 1)
)
```

Large prey that are eaten rarely rank high by weight and low by records; small
prey that are eaten often do the reverse. Neither column is the right one on
its own. If you report only one, say which and why.

## Application 2: how much does the reporting rank change the picture?

The tree holds every rank, so you can compare the leading prey at several
ranks in a few lines:

```{r app-ranks}
for (r in c("Class", "Order", "Family")) {
  tb <- dv_rank_table(tree, r)
  cat("\n", r, ": top 3 by share of prey records\n")
  print(head(tb[, c("label", "pct_occ")], 3), row.names = FALSE)
}
```

Watch for one pattern on real data: two strata that look alike at class can
differ at genus. The change is then happening inside the coarse categories,
and an analysis made only at class would not see it.

## Application 3: how much of the diet was identified?

The unidentified share at a rank tells you how much of the material a
statement at that rank rests on.

```{r app-na}
na_share <- do.call(rbind, lapply(prep$ranks, function(r) {
  lab <- paste0(toupper(substring(r, 1, 1)), substring(r, 2))
  tb  <- dv_rank_table(tree, lab)
  data.frame(rank = lab,
             unidentified_pct = round(sum(tb$pct_occ[tb$label == "NA"]), 1))
}))
na_share
```

If half the records are unidentified at genus, a genus-level statement rests on
the other half. Digestion does not remove prey at random with respect to taxon,
so that half is not a random sample. The vignette "A known diet" shows what
this does on a simulated survey.

## What changes what

| Argument | Where | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `prey_id` / `prey_name` | `dv_spec()` | which key is looked up; the ID is used first |
| `ranks` | `dv_spec()` | the number of rings |
| `covariates` | `dv_spec()` | what you can compare diets across |
| `taxonomy` | `dv_prepare()` | where the hierarchy comes from |
| `fuzzy` | `dv_prepare()` | whether misspelled names can match; the log must then be read |
| `weight_col` | `dv_build_tree()` | whether the weight share exists |
| `count_col` | `dv_build_tree()` | share of prey records becomes the numerical share (%N) |
| `mode` | `dv_sunburst()` | what sizes the wedges |
| `colors` | `dv_sunburst()` | whether colors match across panels; pass one palette |
| `rotation` | `dv_sunburst()` | start angle; keep it the same across panels |
| `breaks` | `dv_add_period()`, `dv_size_bins()` | the strata themselves |
| `by` | `dv_digestion_diagnostic()` | whether the table is split further |
| `cross` | `dv_build_html()` | the panel grid, inner within outer |

## Three things to keep in mind

Every ring holds all the records. A record not identified to a rank still
appears in that rank's ring, as unidentified, so no share is rescaled to the
identified records only, and each ring can be read on its own.

The share of prey records is not %FO. %FO counts stomachs and does not add up
across ranks; `dv_fo_table()` computes it. Name the quantity you report.

A DietView figure can be reproduced from three files: the data, the
specification and the lineage table. Resolve the taxonomy once, read the
report, archive the lineage table, and run everything from that snapshot.

## References

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish
stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. *Fisheries Research*,
196, 126–140.

Scharf, F. S., Juanes, F., & Rountree, R. A. (2000). Predator size–prey size
relationships of marine fish predators: interspecific variation and effects of
ontogeny and body size on trophic-niche breadth. *Marine Ecology Progress
Series*, 208, 229–248.
